segments.english: These are the generations of Ishmael, son of Abraham, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah's maidservant, bore to Abraham.
segments.literal: and-these generations-of Ishmael son-of Abraham who bore Hagar the-Egyptian maidservant-of Sarah to-Abraham

tokens.note: verbless clause: the English supplies 'are' as its copula
construct; the lexicon sense is 'account of a man and his descendants', and it governs the names that follow
qatal in a relative clause; its subject Hagar comes after the verb

phrases.english: These are the generations of Ishmael, son of Abraham,
whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah's maidservant, bore to Abraham.
phrases.literal: who bore Hagar the-Egyptian maidservant-of Sarah to-Abraham

grammar: וְאֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדוֹת is a verbless clause, 'these (are) the generations'; 'are' in the English is the copula.
The etnaḥta on אַבְרָהָם closes the first clause at 'son of Abraham'; the relative clause that follows is set off from it.
יָלְדָה is qatal, 3rd feminine singular, with Hagar named after the verb; the appositions 'the Egyptian' and 'maidservant of Sarah' stand after her name.

commentary.summary: Radak: the Torah records Ishmael's line out of honour to Abraham, his firstborn, and to show that Ishmael had twelve princes, as God told Abraham.
Radak: though Ishmael was the son of a maidservant, Abraham loved him as firstborn; God blessed him for Abraham's sake and prospered him, and he fathered the twelve princes.

context: Hagar was an Egyptian maidservant of Sarah. The giving of a maidservant to a childless wife, so that her children are counted to the wife, is cited from the Nuzi tablets; scholars differ on how closely the Nuzi practice matches Genesis.

segments.english: These are the names of the sons of Ishmael, by their names, according to their generations: the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebaioth, and Kedar, and Adbeel, and Mibsam.
segments.literal: and-these names-of sons-of Ishmael by-their-names to-their-generations firstborn-of Ishmael Nebaioth and-Kedar and-Adbeel and-Mibsam

tokens.note: the same noun as 25:13.2, with the preposition ב and a 3rd masculine plural suffix
לְ with תּוֹלְדוֹת; what the phrase means is disputed (see commentary)
construct of בְּכוֹר; the names that follow are in apposition to it

phrases.english: These are the names of the sons of Ishmael, by their names, according to their generations:
phrases.literal: and-these names-of sons-of Ishmael by-their-names to-their-generations

grammar: The verse opens a list with a verbless clause, 'these (are) the names'; the copula is English.
The etnaḥta on לְתוֹלְדֹתָם closes the heading. The two prepositional phrases 'by their names' and 'to their generations' each have a 3rd masculine plural suffix.
בְּכֹר יִשְׁמָעֵאל is a construct, 'the firstborn of Ishmael'. The first son is named (Nebaioth), and the others follow, each joined by ו.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'by their names, by their generations' means the order of their births, one after another.
Radak: the names are given in the order of their generations, as they were born, the males; the firstborn was Nebaioth.

context: Nebaioth is generally identified with the Nabaiate of the Assyrian royal inscriptions, a people of the north Arabian desert; the identification is not beyond dispute.
Kedar is a tribe of the Arabian desert (Isa. 21:17).

segments.english: and Mishma, and Dumah, and Massa.
grammar: A list of three names, each with ו, and no verb. The list continues from 25:13 and is completed in 25:15.
The accents divide the names: merkha on מִשְׁמָע, tipḥa on דּוּמָה, and silluq on מַשָּׂא, which closes the verse.

segments.english: Hadad, and Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.
grammar: Five names. With the four of 25:13 and the three of 25:14 they make the twelve of 25:16.
ו stands before the second and fifth names only; the English repeats 'and' where the Hebrew does.
The accents munaḥ, zaqef qaton, merkha, tipḥa and silluq each mark one name; silluq ends the verse.

segments.english: These are the sons of Ishmael, and these are their names, in their villages and in their palaces: twelve princes to their tribes.
segments.literal: these they sons-of Ishmael and-these names-of-them in-their-villages and-in-their-palaces two-ten princes to-their-tribes

tokens.note: the pronoun repeats 'these'; 'are' in the English is the copula of the verbless clause
חָצֵר: the lexicon gives 'settled abode, settlement, village'; how the place was built is disputed (see context)
טִירָה: the lexicon gives 'encampment, battlement'. 'Palaces' follows Ibn Ezra, the normative reading; Radak's 'fortified cities' is recorded
the numeral 'twelve' is written as two plus ten
לְ with אֻמָּה; the lamed is taken as 'to' (Ibn Ezra)

phrases.english: These are the sons of Ishmael,
in their villages and in their palaces:

grammar: אֵלֶּה הֵם is a verbless clause; the pronoun הֵם repeats the subject, and 'are' is the English copula.
The second clause, 'and these are their names', is verbless too. The names are those of 25:13 to 15.
The two locatives בְּחַצְרֵיהֶם וּבְטִירֹתָם are parallel, each with ב and a 3rd masculine plural suffix. The etnaḥta on וּבְטִירֹתָם closes them; the numeral and the title come after it.
The numeral is compound, שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר ('two and ten'), with the plural noun נְשִׂיאִם; it stands in apposition to the names above.
segments.note: Palaces follows Ibn Ezra's normative reading of טירות; the lexicon's 'encampment, battlement' and Radak's fortified cities are recorded in commentary. The lamed of לְאֻמֹּתָם is rendered 'to' per Ibn Ezra.

commentary.summary: Radak: the general statement 'these are the sons' comes after the particulars, a usual form in Scripture; the repetition adds clarity.
Rashi: חצרים are large cities without walls, and he takes the Targum's word for them as 'opened places'.
Ibn Ezra: טירות are palaces (ארמונים), like the טירת כסף of the Song of Songs.

Ibn Ezra: the lamed of לְאֻמֹּתָם is an added preposition, like the lamed of לְגוֹיֵיהֶם, not part of the root; the word is the root of 'nation' (as in Gen. 25:23), and the meaning is the same without the lamed.
Radak: the repetition tells the reader that wherever a people is named with one of these names, it is one of Ishmael's sons.
Radak: where their portion fell they lived in greatness, in their ḥatserim (open towns) and their tirot (great cities and fortresses).

Radak: each of the twelve was a prince and the head of a great family named after him, as Jetur Naphish in the war of the Hagrites; Kedar, Dumah, Massa and Tema are each named in the prophets as a separate nation.
Onkelos renders the two locatives as 'open places' (פַּצְחֵיהוֹן) and 'great cities' (כַּרְכֵּיהוֹן).

context: The Hebrew names two kinds of settled place, ḥatserim and tirot. The commentators differ: the ḥatserim are taken as unwalled villages (Radak) or large towns without walls (Rashi), and the tirot as fortified cities (Radak) or palaces (Ibn Ezra). The commentary records the positions.
The twelve names are identified with tribes of the north Arabian desert and its edge; each identification of a name with a known people is a scholarly proposal and is disputed.

segments.english: These are the years of the life of Ishmael, a hundred and thirty-seven years; and he expired, and he died, and he was gathered to his people.
segments.literal: and-these years-of life-of Ishmael hundred years and-thirty years and-seven years and-he-expired and-he-died and-he-was-gathered to his-people

tokens.note: the form is parsed as the dual construct of שָׁנָה; the phrase reads 'the years of the life of'
a hundred as part of a larger number (137)
before a singular noun (שָׁנָה)
wayyiqtol: the verb series continues the sequence
wayyiqtol
idiom for death: 'gathered to his people' (see context)
עַם: the lexicon gives 'kinsman'; 'people' is the plain sense of the idiom

phrases.english: These are the years of the life of Ishmael,

phrases.literal: hundred years and-thirty years and-seven years

phrases.english: and he expired, and he died,
and he was gathered to his people.

grammar: The age is given as three sums in sequence, a hundred years, and thirty years, and seven years; the English adds them as one figure, and the literal keeps the Hebrew's three.
Three wayyiqtol verbs, וַיִּגְוַע וַיָּמָת וַיֵּאָסֶף, carry the sequence: 'expired', 'died', and the idiom of being gathered to one's people.
The etnaḥta on שָׁנִים closes the clause of the age; the silluq on עַמָּיו closes the verse.

commentary.summary: Rashi (midrash): asks why Ishmael's years are counted, so that Jacob's years can be set against them; Jacob spent fourteen years in Eber's house before he left his father, since Ishmael died when Jacob left.
Rashi: the verb גְּוִיעָה is said only of the righteous.

Ramban: the plain sense is that the text gives the years of the righteous' offspring to show that the seed of the righteous is blessed; of the midrash's reasons for Ishmael's years, he finds most correct that Ishmael repented.
Ramban: גְּוִיעָה is death without painful illness or suffering, which only the righteous obtain; where the verb stands beside 'died' or 'gathered', it points to a righteous death.
Radak: the years are recorded in Abraham's honour; the rabbis record them only to compare Jacob's years.
Onkelos renders וַיִּגְוַע as וְאִתְנְגִיד, which Ramban glosses as a swoon (עִלּוּף).

context: 'Gathered to his people' (וַיֵּאָסֶף אֶל־עַמָּיו) is the Hebrew idiom for death; by itself it does not describe a burial.

segments.english: And they dwelt from Havilah as far as Shur, which is before Egypt, as you go toward Asshur; he fell before all his brothers.
segments.literal: and-they-dwelt from-Havilah as-far-as Shur which upon face-of Egypt in-your-coming Asshur-ward; upon face-of all his-brothers fell

tokens.note: wayyiqtol, 3rd masculine plural; the subject is Ishmael's sons
על פְּנֵי is one idiom; the English 'before' belongs to the whole phrase
infinitive construct with a 2nd masculine singular suffix by the parse, in a narrative with no addressee; the form is a crux (see apparatus). The English keeps 'you' as the suffix gives it
the directional ה on אַשּׁוּר
עַל פְּנֵי כָל־אֶחָיו: the idiom 'before all his brothers'
qatal after a wayyiqtol series: a separate statement; the sense of נָפַל is disputed (see commentary)

phrases.english: And they dwelt from Havilah as far as Shur,
he fell before all his brothers.

grammar: The verse is a wayyiqtol (וַיִּשְׁכְּנוּ) with the boundary formula 'from Havilah as far as Shur', then a relative clause placing Shur 'before Egypt', then a second boundary phrase, 'toward Asshur'.
בֹּאֲכָה has a 2nd masculine singular suffix by the parse, while the narrative is in the third person; the English keeps the suffix, 'as you go', and the literal keeps 'your'.

נָפָל is a qatal after a wayyiqtol series, so it reads as a separate statement rather than the next step of the dwelling. The third masculine singular is unnamed; the English 'he' is the person of the form.
The etnaḥta on אַשּׁוּרָה closes the first half at Asshur, and the silluq on נָפָֽל closes the verse. The paragraph mark (פ) after it ends the section.
segments.note: English 'fell' keeps the verb. Rashi, Radak and Onkelos read 'dwelt', and Ibn Ezra offers three readings (lot, movement, death in a brother's lifetime); all are recorded in commentary, since the words do not settle the sense. 'Before' is the idiom על פני, which leaves Ibn Ezra's death reading open without choosing it.

commentary.summary: Rashi: נָפָל here means 'dwelt' (שָׁכַן), as in the Midianites and Amalekites who lay in the valley (Judg. 7:12). He notes Gen. 16:12, 'before all his brothers he shall dwell': before Abraham died Ishmael dwelt, and after Abraham died he fell.
Ibn Ezra: 'all his brothers' (על פני כל אחיו) are Zimran and Jokshan.

Ibn Ezra gives three readings of נָפָל: his portion or lot fell to him; most of Ishmael's sons moved from place to place, as in 'to the Chaldeans you fall' (Jer. 37:13); or the verse speaks of Ishmael's death in one brother's lifetime, since the cause of his death is not known. He finds the second a little far, since his brothers are in the east and Egypt and Asshur are west of the Land.
Radak: the sons and their generations dwelt from Havilah to Shur, for there their portion fell to them.
Radak: the phrase 'before all his brothers' is as the angel told Hagar, 'before all his brothers he shall dwell' (Gen. 16:12); the comment is cut off in the pack.
Radak: נָפָל means 'dwelt', as in 'lying in the valley' (Judg. 7:12).
Onkelos renders נָפָל as שְׁרָא, 'dwelt'.

apparatus: בֹּאֲכָה: the parse gives a 2nd masculine singular suffix, against the third-person narrative; the form is a crux, and the English keeps 'you' as the suffix gives it.
context: Havilah is a name also used in the table of nations for a land; scholars disagree on whether this Havilah is the same place, and its location is not fixed.
Shur is the desert on the route from Canaan to Egypt; here it is located by its position before Egypt.
Asshur is Assyria, the land on the upper Tigris, in the Mesopotamian sense of the name.
